<reason>Both sides argued the motion as written and stayed disciplined on evidence. PRO built a coherent mechanism (wage-SSNIP, ex ante vs ex post remedies, worker-dollar-equals-consumer-dollar) and landed a memorable closing line that CON's "never outweigh" rule is the asymmetry restated rather than defended. But CON progressively narrowed the debate to the case that actually decides the motion—the genuine conflict between measured price gains and labor harm—and PRO never supplied a way to resolve it beyond "condition it," which CON plausibly showed is already what "counting" does. CON also extracted a concession that the wage test rarely bites outside licensed, geographically locked workers, then argued those one-hospital-town cases are already caught on the price side; PRO's closing did not engage that redundancy point substantively. CON's answers to PRO's pressure questions were direct and turned them (quit-to-whom → price review already catches the single-seller merger), while PRO's answers, though direct, effectively conceded the screen logic CON then reclaimed. A clear but competitive CON edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's A4.4/A4.5 response to PRO's "quit to whom" question: if two hospitals merge into one buyer of nurses, they also merge into one seller of care, so price-side review already blocks it; any scarcity surviving price review is scarcity the merger didn't create. PRO's closing labeled this "someone else's job" but never rebutted the redundancy, leaving parity's marginal value unestablished in PRO's own strongest example.</best_rebuttal>
